comparison: Both strongly support the forebrain Prlr deletion findings (C1, C29-C36, C63, C89). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation while peer reviewers unanimously praise the study design and data quality, with all three reviewers affirming the conclusions are well-supported.

OpenEval finds claims C37-C41 supported with appropriate statistical evidence showing prolactin (not progesterone) suppresses LH secretion. Peer Reviewer 1 expresses uncertainty about the progesterone findings, noting surprise given effectiveness of progesterone-containing birth control in lactating women, questioning generalizability rather than the data itself.

Complete agreement on the longitudinal photometry study (C42-C56, C66-C67, C70-C71). Both recognize this as a major technical achievement - OpenEval notes it's the first longitudinal study in same animals with appropriate statistics, while all three peer reviewers praise it as technically impressive, exemplary, and demonstrating exceptional skill.

Both support the kisspeptin-specific Prlr deletion findings (C7, C57-C61, C68, C79-C80, C90). OpenEval emphasizes the specificity and statistical rigor. Peer reviewers support the conclusion with minor caveats, noting prolactin action on Kiss1 neurons is 'at least partially responsible' for lactational infertility.

Divergent evaluations of incomplete deletion effects (C85-C87). OpenEval finds the comparison and acknowledgment of limitations appropriate though speculative. Peer Reviewer 1 identifies this as a significant weakness, questioning whether partial maintenance of cyclicity is due to incomplete deletion or involvement of other factors.

Both evaluate pregnancy-related progesterone mechanisms (C72-C76). OpenEval rates as uncertain, noting reasonable interpretations but lack of direct validation and tension with mifepristone data. Peer Reviewer 1 positively receives this as offering insight into postpartum ovulation, likely to inspire future testing.

Complete agreement on methodological strengths (C83-C84). Both recognize the advantage of maintaining normal lactation/suckling and avoiding dopamine agonists. OpenEval notes this as a legitimate methodological strength; Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly affirms this isolated the effects of prolactin.

Divergent evaluations of broader implications (C88, C81-C82). OpenEval rates speculation about hyperprolactinemia across species as uncertain without direct evidence. Peer Reviewer 1 raises significant concerns about generalizability, providing specific examples from rats, humans, and rhesus monkeys where results differ, suggesting mice may be an outlier.

OpenEval evaluates comparison to historical LH patterns (C77-C78) as supported, noting valid integration of current photometry findings with prior literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific historical comparison.

OpenEval evaluates background/context claims (C9-C28, C69) as supported with appropriate citations to established literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers focused on novel findings rather than background material.

Both address the SE-LH pulse correlation (C91). OpenEval includes this in comprehensive evaluation of longitudinal photometry data as strongly supported (p≤0.0001, 73/73 events). Peer reviewers implicitly accept this technical validation through praise of photometry methodology, with Reviewer 3 noting methods are advanced and appropriate.

Both address maintenance of normal lactation (C33-C34, C58). OpenEval includes this as part of comprehensive forebrain deletion evaluation showing intact suckling/lactation. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as a study strength, with Reviewer 1 noting it isolated prolactin effects by maintaining normal lactation and suckling.

Peer review addresses C65 (not in OpenEval results) as part of progesterone evaluation. Reviewer 1 questions progesterone findings given effectiveness in human birth control, raising concerns about interpretation or generalizability not captured in OpenEval's claim-level analysis.
